text:
The Long Way Home

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. Jim Lovell, the commander, was a veteran of three earlier flights and was making his fourth trip into space. Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, was a newcomer to spaceflight. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days before. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and was grounded by the flight surgeons. Swigert stepped in after a frantic few days of training. Nobody watching the launch could have guessed that this substitution would become one of many small turns of fortune in a story that would end very differently from the way it began.

The mission was meant to be the third landing on the Moon. By then the public had grown used to the spectacle. Television networks gave the flight little attention, and for the first two days it went about as smoothly as any crew could hope. The astronauts called their command module Odyssey and their lunar lander Aquarius. They coasted outward, and on the evening of April 13 they were nearly 200,000 miles from home. Mission Control asked Swigert to switch on the fans in the oxygen tanks, a routine chore that stirred the supercold liquid inside so the gauges would read accurately.

A little before ten that night, Houston time, Swigert flipped the switches. Moments later the crew heard a loud bang and felt the spacecraft shudder. Warning lights flared across the panel. Swigert radioed down that they had a problem, and Lovell repeated it in the calm phrasing that has been quoted ever since. At first the men on the ground suspected faulty instruments. The truth was far worse. Oxygen tank number two had exploded inside the service module, the bulky cylinder behind the crew cabin that held their power and life support. The blast had torn away a panel, crippled the second tank and left the spacecraft venting its supply into space.

The cause traced back years. The tank had been dropped slightly during handling in 1965, and the damage had gone unnoticed. During a ground test before launch, technicians had trouble draining it, and they used heaters to boil off the oxygen. The heaters ran far hotter than the thermostat switches were built to survive, and the switches fused shut. Inside the tank, the insulation on the wiring was left bare and brittle. When Swigert turned on the stirring fan, a spark leapt across the wires and ignited the oxygen and the Teflon around it. Pressure climbed until the tank burst.

Within minutes the fuel cells that made electricity and water began to die. Odyssey was losing its lifeblood. Lovell looked out a window and saw gas streaming into space, and he knew the Moon was no longer the goal. Flight director Gene Kranz and his teams in Houston turned their whole effort toward a single purpose, which was getting three men home alive. The lunar module Aquarius, designed to carry two men to the surface for a couple of days, became their lifeboat. The crew shut down the command module to save what little battery power remained, then crowded into the lander and brought it to life.

The first decision was about the route. The spacecraft was on a path that would have swung it around the Moon and returned it to Earth, but it would have missed by a wide margin. Controllers considered turning back at once, but the main engine on the damaged service module could not be trusted, and a sudden reversal would have been risky. They chose to swing around the far side of the Moon and fire the lander's descent engine to speed the return. That burn came a couple of hours after the closest approach. As the crew rounded the Moon, they passed farther from Earth than any humans had ever travelled, a record that still stands. They had little time to enjoy the view. Haise and Lovell took a few photographs, and then the work resumed.

Life aboard Aquarius became a trial of endurance. The lander had been designed for two men for two days, and now it held three for four. Power was strictly limited, so almost everything was turned off. The cabin temperature sank toward freezing, and condensation beaded on the walls. The men wore their flight clothes and then, when they could not stay warm, pulled on whatever else they had. Water was rationed to a few ounces a day to keep the lander's electronics cool. Haise developed a fever and a painful infection. Sleep was almost impossible. Lovell lost about fourteen pounds, and the crew together shed a total of nearly thirty.

A deadlier problem emerged in the air itself. Every breath the men exhaled added carbon dioxide to the cabin, and the filters in the lander were filling up. Spare filters existed in the command module, but they were square, and the lander's sockets were round. On the ground, engineers gathered the same items the crew had on board, including plastic bags, cardboard, a spacesuit hose and a great deal of duct tape. They built an adapter and read the instructions up to the crew, who copied the design. The improvised device worked. Carbon dioxide levels fell, and the men could breathe again.

Meanwhile, the course needed correcting. The lander's guidance system had no use for the star sightings the crew normally relied on, because the debris cloud around the ship glittered like a field of fireflies. Lovell used the sunlit edge of the Earth to line up the spacecraft, and the crew fired the descent engine by hand for a burn lasting about fourteen seconds. Later they needed another small adjustment, again aimed by eye. These burns kept them in the narrow corridor into the atmosphere. Too shallow, and the ship would skip off like a stone. Too steep, and it would burn up.

The next puzzle belonged to the engineers. Odyssey had to be restarted after days of cold, with only a limited reserve of battery power, and nobody had ever written a procedure for doing it in this way. Mattingly, the astronaut who had been left behind, spent long hours in a simulator working out a sequence that would use the fewest amps. He and the others finally had a checklist that worked, and it was read up to the crew word by word.

On the morning of April 17, the men made their final preparations. They released the damaged service module first, and for the first time they saw the harm. A whole side panel was gone, and the equipment inside was torn and scorched. Lovell described it to the ground. Then they said goodbye to Aquarius, which had saved their lives, and let it drift away to burn up in the atmosphere. Odyssey was alone, and the three men sat in a cabin that was cold and damp, waiting for the heat of reentry.

Radio silence is part of every return, because the superheated air around the capsule blocks signals. This time the blackout seemed to last longer than expected, and the control room waited in strained silence. After an extra minute, the voice of Swigert came through. Parachutes bloomed against the sky, and a few minutes later the capsule settled into the South Pacific near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship Iwo Jima. The mission had lasted almost six days. The men were tired and unwell but safe.

A review board later pinned down the cause, and engineers redesigned the oxygen tanks and their wiring. The flight never reached the Moon, yet many came to call it a successful failure. It showed what trained people could do when a plan collapsed, and it remains a lesson in calm, improvisation and the value of working together under pressure.
